{{Short description|Computational problem of graph theory}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''k'' shortest path routing}}
The '''''k'' shortest path routing''' problem is a generalization of the [[Shortest-path routing|shortest path routing problem]] in a given [[Network theory|network.]] It asks not only about a shortest path but also about next ''k−1'' shortest paths (which may be longer than the shortest path). A variation of the problem is the loopless ''k'' shortest paths.

Finding ''k'' shortest paths is possible by extending [[Dijkstra's algorithm]] or the [[Bellman–Ford algorithm|Bellman-Ford algorithm]].{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

== History ==
Since 1957, many papers have been published on the ''k'' shortest path routing problem. Most of the fundamental works were done between 1960s and 2001. Since then, most of the research has been on the problem's applications and its variants. In 2010, Michael Günther et al. published a book on ''Symbolic calculation of ''k''-shortest paths and related measures with the stochastic process algebra tool CASPA''.<ref>{{cite conference | last1=Günther | first1=Michael | last2=Schuster | first2=Johann | last3=Siegle | first3=Markus | title=Symbolic calculation of ''k''-shortest paths and related measures with the stochastic process algebra tool CASPA | chapter=Symbolic calculation of k-shortest paths and related measures with the stochastic process algebra tool CASPA | publisher=ACM | date=2010-04-27 | page= | isbn=978-1-60558-916-9 | doi=10.1145/1772630.1772635 | pages=13–18}}</ref>

== Algorithm ==

Dijkstra's algorithm can be generalized to find the ''k'' shortest paths.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

{| class="wikitable"
|-
| '''Definitions''':
:* '''G(V, E)''': weighted directed graph, with set of [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]]  '''V'''  and set of directed  [[edge (geometry)|edges]] '''E''',
:* '''w(u, v)''': cost of  directed edge from node '''u''' to node '''v''' (costs are non-negative).
:Links that do not satisfy constraints on the shortest path are removed from the graph
:* '''s''': the source node
:* '''t''': the destination node
:* '''''K''''': the number of shortest paths to find
:* '''p<sub>u</sub>''': a path from '''s''' to '''u'''
:* '''B''' is a heap data structure containing paths
:* '''P''': set of shortest paths from '''s''' to '''t'''
:* '''count<sub>u</sub>''': number of shortest paths found to  node '''u'''

'''Algorithm:'''

::'''P''' =empty,
:: '''count<sub>u</sub>''' = 0,  for all u in V
:: insert path '''p<sub>s</sub>''' = {s} into '''B''' with cost '''0'''
:: while '''B''' is not empty and '''count<sub>t</sub>''' < '''K''':
:::– let '''p<sub>u</sub>''' be the shortest cost path in '''B''' with cost '''C'''
:::– '''B''' = '''B''' − '''{p<sub>u</sub> }''', '''count<sub>u</sub>''' = '''count<sub>u</sub>''' + 1
:::– if '''u''' = '''t''' then '''P''' = '''P''' U '''{p<sub>u</sub>}'''
:::– if '''count<sub>u</sub>'''  ≤ '''K''' then
::::* for each vertex '''v''' adjacent to '''u''':
:::::– let '''p<sub>v</sub>''' be a new path with cost '''C''' + '''w(u, v)''' formed by concatenating edge '''(u, v)''' to path '''p<sub>u</sub>'''
:::::– insert '''p<sub>v</sub>''' into '''B'''
:: return '''P'''
|-
|
|}

== Variations ==

There are two main variations of the ''k'' shortest path routing problem.  In one variation, paths are allowed to visit the same node more than once, thus creating loops.  In another variation, paths are required to be [[simple graph|simple and loopless]].  The loopy version is solvable using Eppstein's algorithm<ref name = Eppstein /> and the loopless variation is solvable by [[Yen's algorithm]].<ref name="Yen">{{cite journal|last=Yen|first=J. Y.|year=1971|title=Finding the ''k''-Shortest Loopless Paths in a Network|journal=[[Management Science (journal)|Management Science]]|volume=1 7|issue=11|pages=712–716|doi=10.1287/mnsc.17.11.712}}.</ref><ref name = Bouillet>{{cite book|title = Path Routing in Mesh Optical Networks|first1 = Eric|last1 = Bouillet|first2 = Georgios|last2 = Ellinas|first3 = Jean-Francois|last3 = Labourdette|first4 = Ramu|last4 = Ramamurthy|publisher = [[John Wiley & Sons]]|year = 2007|isbn = 9780470015650|chapter = Path Routing &ndash; Part 2: Heuristics|chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=zSSjFf-jZT8C&pg=PG129|pages = 125–138}}</ref>

=== Loopy variant ===

In this variant, the problem is simplified by not requiring paths to be loopless.<ref name = Bouillet />  A solution was given by B. L. Fox in 1975 in which the ''k''-shortest paths are determined in {{nowrap|''O''(''m'' + ''kn'' log ''n'')}} [[asymptotic time complexity]] (using [[big O notation|big ''O'' notation]]).<ref>{{cite journal|title = ''K''th shortest paths and applications to the probabilistic networks|first = B. L.|last = Fox|journal = [[Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences|ORSA/TIMS Joint National Meeting]]|volume = 23|page = B263|year = 1975}} [[CiNii|CiNii National Article ID]]: 10012857200.</ref>  In 1998, [[David Eppstein]] reported an approach that maintains an asymptotic complexity of {{nowrap|''O''(''m'' + ''n'' log&nbsp;''n'' + ''k'')}} by computing an implicit representation of the paths, each of which can be output in ''O''(''n'') extra time.<ref name = Eppstein>{{cite journal|first = David|last = Eppstein|authorlink = David Eppstein|title = Finding the ''k'' Shortest Paths|year = 1998|journal = [[SIAM J. Comput.]]|url = https://www.ics.uci.edu/~eppstein/pubs/Epp-SJC-98.pdf|volume = 28|issue = 2|pages = 652–673|doi = 10.1137/S0097539795290477}}</ref><ref name = Bouillet /> In 2015, Akiba ''et al.'' devised an indexing method as a significantly faster alternative for Eppstein's algorithm, in which a data structure called an index is constructed from a graph and then top-''k'' distances between arbitrary pairs of vertices can be rapidly obtained.<ref>{{cite book|first1 = Takuya|last1 = Akiba|first2 = Takanori|last2 = Hayashi|first3 = Nozomi|last3 = Nori|first4 = Yoichi|last4 = Iwata|first5 = Yuichi|last5 = Yoshida|chapter = Efficient Top-''k'' Shortest-Path Distance Queries on Large Networks by Pruned Landmark Labeling|title = Proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence|chapter-url = https://www.aaai.org/ocs/index.php/AAAI/AAAI15/paper/view/9320/9217|date = January 2015|location = Austin, TX|pages = 2–8|url = https://www.aaai.org/ocs/index.php/AAAI/AAAI15/schedConf/presentations|publisher = [[Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence]]}}</ref>

=== Loopless variant ===

In the loopless variant, the paths are forbidden to contain loops, which adds an additional level of complexity.<ref name = Bouillet /> It can be solved using [[Yen's algorithm]]<ref name="Yen" /><ref name = Bouillet /> to find the lengths of all shortest paths from a fixed node to all other nodes in an ''n''-node non negative-distance network, a technique requiring only 2''n''<sup>2</sup> additions and ''n''<sup>2</sup> comparison, fewer than other available [[shortest path algorithms]] need.  The running time complexity is [[Pseudo-polynomial time|pseudo-polynomial]], being {{nowrap|''O''(''kn''(''m'' + ''n'' log ''n''))}} (where ''m'' and ''n'' represent the number of edges and vertices, respectively).<ref name = Yen /><ref name = Bouillet /> In 2007, [[John Hershberger]] and [[Subhash Suri]] proposed a replacement paths algorithm, a more efficient implementation of Lawler's <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lawler|first=Eugene L.|date=1972-03-01|title=A Procedure for Computing the K Best Solutions to Discrete Optimization Problems and Its Application to the Shortest Path Problem|url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/mnsc.18.7.401|journal=Management Science|volume=18|issue=7|pages=401–405|doi=10.1287/mnsc.18.7.401|issn=0025-1909|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and Yen's algorithm with ''O''(''n'') improvement in time for a large number of graphs, but not all of them (therefore not changing the asymptotic bound of Yen's algorithm).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hershberger|first1=John|last2=Maxel|first2=Matthew|last3=Suri|first3=Subhash|year=2007|title=Finding the ''k'' Shortest Simple Paths: A New Algorithm and its Implementation|url=https://archive.siam.org/meetings/alenex03/Abstracts/jhershberger.pdf|journal=[[ACM Transactions on Algorithms]]|volume=3|issue=4|at=Article 45 (19 pages)|doi=10.1145/1290672.1290682|s2cid=10703503 |authorlink1=John Hershberger|authorlink3=Subhash Suri}}</ref>

== Some examples and description ==

=== Example 1 ===

The following example makes use of Yen's model to find ''k'' shortest paths between communicating end nodes. That is, it finds a shortest path, second shortest path, etc. up to the K<sup>th</sup> shortest path. More details can be found [http://www.technical-recipes.com/2012/the-k-shortest-paths-algorithm-in-c/#more-2432 here].
The code provided in this example attempts to solve the ''k'' shortest path routing problem for a 15-nodes network containing a combination of unidirectional and bidirectional links:
[[File:15-node network containing a combination of bi-directional and uni-directional links.png|thumbnail|15-node network containing a combination of bi-directional and uni-directional links]]

=== Example 2 ===

Another example is the use of ''k'' shortest paths algorithm to track multiple objects. The technique implements a multiple object tracker based on the ''k'' shortest paths routing algorithm. A set of probabilistic occupancy maps is used as input. An object detector provides the input.

The complete details can be found at "[http://cvlab.epfl.ch/software/ksp/ Computer Vision Laboratory] – CVLAB".

=== Example 3 ===

Another use of ''k'' shortest paths algorithms is to design a transit network that enhances passengers' experience in public transportation systems. Such an example of a transit network can be constructed by putting traveling time under consideration. In addition to traveling time, other conditions may be taken depending upon economical and geographical limitations. Despite variations in parameters, the ''k'' shortest path algorithms finds the most optimal solutions that satisfies almost all user needs. Such applications of ''k'' shortest path algorithms are becoming common, recently Xu, He, Song, and Chaudhry (2012) studied the ''k'' shortest path problems in transit network systems.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Xu | first1=Wangtu | last2=He | first2=Shiwei | last3=Song | first3=Rui | last4=Chaudhry | first4=Sohail S. | title=Finding the ''k'' shortest paths in a schedule-based transit network | journal=Computers & Operations Research | volume=39 | issue=8 | date=2012 | doi=10.1016/j.cor.2010.02.005 | pages=1812–1826| s2cid=29232689 }}</ref>

== Applications ==

The ''k'' shortest path routing is a good alternative for:

:*[http://raweb.inria.fr/rapportsactivite/RA2009/aspi/uid62.html Geographic path planning]
:* Network routing, especially in [[optical mesh network]] where there are additional constraints that cannot be solved by using [[Shortest path algorithms|ordinary shortest path algorithms]].
:*[[Computational linguistics|Hypothesis generation in computational linguistics]]
:*[https://web.archive.org/web/20120506201524/http://bioinformatics.oxfordjournals.org/content/21/16/3401.full.pdf?keytype=ref&ijkey=LBKAnjRh0mW0xP4 Sequence alignment and metabolic pathway finding in bioinformatics]
:*[https://web.archive.org/web/20130108024800/http://cvlab.epfl.ch/publications/publications/2011/BerclazFTF11.pdf Multiple object tracking] as described above
:* Road Networks: road junctions are the nodes (vertices) and each  edge (link) of the graph is associated with a road segment between two junctions.

== Related problems ==

*The [[Breadth-first search|breadth-first search algorithm]] is used when the search is only limited to two operations.
*The [[Floyd–Warshall algorithm]] solves all pairs shortest paths.
*[[Johnson's algorithm]] solves all pairs' shortest paths, and may be faster than Floyd–Warshall on [[sparse graph]]s.
*[[Perturbation theory]] finds (at worst) the locally shortest path.
Cherkassky et al.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Cherkassky | first1=Boris V. | last2=Goldberg | first2=Andrew V. |author-link2=Andrew V. Goldberg | last3=Radzik | first3=Tomasz | title=Shortest paths algorithms: Theory and experimental evaluation | journal=Mathematical Programming | volume=73 | issue=2 | date=1996 | issn=0025-5610 | doi=10.1007/BF02592101 | pages=129–174| bibcode=1996MatPr..73..129C | s2cid=414427 }}</ref> provide more algorithms and associated evaluations.
